interfaces.name: Pivotal
interfaces.type_shape: Common law under every null distribution, not merely common expectation. Exact e-variables need not be pivotal.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Common law under every null distribution, not merely common expectation. Exact e-variables need not be pivotal.

members.statement_original: A random variable $X$ is pivotal for $\mathcal P$ if $X$ has the same distribution under all $P\in\mathcal P$.

interfaces.name: E-variable
interfaces.type_shape: Preserve four separate notions: null validity, exactness, expectation nontriviality, and pointwise positive log e-power. Uniform infimum-positive e-power in T6.7 is strictly stronger.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Preserve four separate notions: null validity, exactness, expectation nontriviality, and pointwise positive log e-power. Uniform infimum-positive e-power in T6.7 is strictly stronger.

members.statement_original: A nonnegative random variable $X$ is a e-variable for $\mathcal P$ if $\mathbb E^P[X]\le1$ for all $P\in\mathcal P$. An e-variable $X$ for $\mathcal P$ is exact if $\mathbb E^P[X]=1$ for all $P\in\mathcal P$. We say $X$ is nontrivial for $\mathcal Q$ if $\mathbb E^Q[X]>1$ for all $Q\in\mathcal Q$. An e-variable $X$ for $\mathcal P$ is said to have nontrivial e-power against $\mathcal Q$ if for each $Q\in\mathcal Q$, $\mathbb E^Q[\log X]>0$.

interfaces.name: P-variable
interfaces.type_shape: Validity and exactness under every null; under each alternative all thresholds have at least nominal rejection probability and some threshold has strict improvement. The improving threshold may depend on Q.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Validity and exactness under every null; under each alternative all thresholds have at least nominal rejection probability and some threshold has strict improvement. The improving threshold may depend on Q.

members.statement_original: A nonnegative random variable $X$ is a p-variable for $\mathcal P$ if $P(X\le\alpha)\le\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $P\in\mathcal P$, and a p-variable $X$ is exact if $P(X\le\alpha)=\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $P\in\mathcal P$. A p-variable $X$ for $\mathcal P$ is nontrivial (or has nontrivial power) against $\mathcal Q$ if, for each $Q\in\mathcal Q$, $Q(X\le\alpha)\ge\alpha$ for all $\alpha\in(0,1)$ with strict inequality for some $\alpha\in(0,1)$. Without loss of generality, p-variables can be restricted to $[0,1]$ by truncation, without changing their properties.

interfaces.name: Convex hull and span
interfaces.type_shape: Ordinary finite convex hull and linear span. Do not insert closures into finite-hypothesis results or identify span with convex hull; signed linear combinations are relevant in the later closure formulation.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Ordinary finite convex hull and linear span. Do not insert closures into finite-hypothesis results or identify span with convex hull; signed linear combinations are relevant in the later closure formulation.

members.statement_original: For a finite set $A$ of random variables or probability measures on the same space, we define $\operatorname{Conv}A$ and $\operatorname{Span}A$ in the usual sense of convex hull and span.

interfaces.name: Convex order
interfaces.type_shape: Convex-integral order on finite first-moment measures, also applied to subprobabilities. Affine test functions entail equal mass and first moment where defined; this is not ordinary setwise measure order.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Convex-integral order on finite first-moment measures, also applied to subprobabilities. Affine test functions entail equal mass and first moment where defined; this is not ordinary setwise measure order.

interfaces.name: Barycenter
interfaces.type_shape: Normalized barycenter of a finite measure, not an unnormalized first moment. The zero-measure case is not specified in this printed definition; record that when SHINE splits an empty component.

members.statement_original: All measures we consider will be finite and have a finite first moment, i.e., $\int|x|\mu(dx)<\infty$. For a Polish space $\mathcal X$, we let $\mathcal M(\mathcal X)$ be the set of all finite measures on $\mathcal X$ and $\Pi(\mathcal X)$ be the set of probability measures on $\mathcal X$. For $\mu\in\mathcal M(\mathbb R^d)$, we denote its barycenter by $\operatorname{bary}(\mu):=\int_{\mathbb R^d}x\mu(dx)/\mu(\mathbb R^d)$.

interfaces.type_shape: The positive diagonal includes zero. Vector diagonal measures and scalar first-coordinate martingales must remain distinct. U1 is the unit-interval uniform probability measure.

members.statement_original: Bold symbols such as $\mathbf x$ and $\boldsymbol\alpha$ will typically denote vectors. Write $\mathbf1_d=(1,\ldots,1)\in\mathbb R^d$, $\mathbf0_d=(0,\ldots,0)\in\mathbb R^d$, $\mathcal I_d=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^d\mid x_1=\cdots=x_d\}=\mathbb R\mathbf1_d$, and $\mathcal I_d^+=\{\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^d\mid x_1=\cdots=x_d\ge0\}=\mathbb R_+\mathbf1_d$. When the dimension $d$ is clear, we may omit the subscript $d$ and write $\mathbf1,\mathbf0,\mathcal I,\mathcal I^+$ instead. We let $U_1$ denote the Lebesgue measure on $[0,1]$. members.statement_original: Consider a tuple of probability measures $\boldsymbol\mu=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_d)$ on a Polish space $\mathcal X$. We say that $\boldsymbol\mu$ is jointly atomless if there exists $\mu\gg\sum_{i=1}^d\mu_i$ and a random variable $\xi$ such that under $\mu$, $\xi$ is atomless and independent of $(d\mu_1/d\mu,\ldots,d\mu_d/d\mu)$.

interfaces.name: E-power
interfaces.type_shape: Optimization over exact pivotal e-variables for a fixed simple alternative. Do not replace by maximizing ordinary expectation, or remove pivotality because another e-value construction does so.

members.statement_original:
The e-power of an e-variable $X$ can be measured by $\mathbb E^Q[\log X]$, which has long been a popular criterion; see for example Kelly (1956); Breiman (1961); Bell and Cover (1988); Shafer et al. (2011); Grünwald, de Heide and Koolen (2024); Waudby-Smith and Ramdas (2024). It has been recently called the e-power of $X$ (Vovk and Wang (2024)), a term we continue to use for simplicity. In this section, we will fix $\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_L\}$ and $\mathcal Q=\{Q\}$. Our goal is to solve
\[
\max\quad\mathbb E^Q[\log X],\qquad\text{s.t.}\quad X:X\text{ is a pivotal exact e-variable}.
\]
(3)

members.statement_original: Suppose that instead of one data point, we observe $n$ iid data points $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ in the space $\mathcal X$ from the experiment. The e-variable is built based on the $n$ data points together instead of a single data point. In other words, given $\mathcal P=\{P_1,\ldots,P_L\}$ and $\mathcal Q=\{Q\}$, we build an e-variable for $\mathcal P^n:=\{P_1^n,\ldots,P_L^n\}$ that is pivotal, exact, and has nontrivial e-power against $\mathcal Q^n:=\{Q^n\}$.

members.statement_original:
Start with $\mu^{(0)}=\delta_{\mathbf1}$, $x_1^{(0)}=1$, and $\mu_1^{(0)}=\gamma$ from (4). At step $s\ge0$, we are given $\mu^{(s)}$, $\{x_k^{(s)}\}_{1\le k\le2^s}$, and $\{\mu_k^{(s)}\}_{1\le k\le2^s}$. For each $k$, we apply Proposition 4.3 to the sub-probability measure $\mu_k^{(s)}$ at the point $x_k^{(s)}$. This yields a unique decomposition of $\mu_k^{(s)}$ into two measures, each having a barycenter on $\mathcal I^+$. Denote them by $\mu_{2k-1}^{(s+1)}$ and $\mu_{2k}^{(s+1)}$. For $1\le k\le2^{s+1}$, define $x_k^{(s+1)}=\operatorname{bary}(\mu_k^{(s+1)})$. Finally, let $\mu^{(s+1)}$ be the probability measure having mass $\mu_k^{(s+1)}(\mathbb R^L)$ on $x_k^{(s+1)}$ for every $k$, i.e.,
\[
\mu^{(s+1)}:=\sum_{k=1}^{2^{s+1}}\mu_k^{(s+1)}(\mathbb R^L)\delta_{x_k^{(s+1)}}.
\]
(11)
The output of the SHINE construction at step $s$ is the measure $\mu^{(s)}$.

interfaces.name: SHINE martingale
interfaces.type_shape: Scalar first-coordinate martingale coupled along the split tree; its reciprocal corresponds to the e-variable. EP_k uses minus log X_k. The theorem wording about almost-sure convergence of measures is interpreted via this coupling, not silently rewritten.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Scalar first-coordinate martingale coupled along the split tree; its reciprocal corresponds to the e-variable. EP_k uses minus log X_k. The theorem wording about almost-sure convergence of measures is interpreted via this coupling, not silently rewritten.

members.statement_original:
Define $\{X_s\}$ as the coupling of the first coordinate of $\{\mu^{(s)}\}$ such that $X_0=1$ and at each $s\ge0$, for $j=2k-1,2k$,
\[
\mathbb P[X_{s+1}=x_j^{(s+1)}\mid X_s=x_k^{(s)}]=\frac{\mu_j^{(s+1)}(\mathbb R^L)}{\mu_{2k-1}^{(s+1)}(\mathbb R^L)+\mu_{2k}^{(s+1)}(\mathbb R^L)}.
\]
(12)
By construction,
\[
x_{2k-1}^{(s+1)}\mu_{2k-1}^{(s+1)}(\mathbb R^L)+x_{2k}^{(s+1)}\mu_{2k}^{(s+1)}(\mathbb R^L)=x_k^{(s)}\mu_k^{(s)}(\mathbb R^L)=x_k^{(s)}(\mu_{2k-1}^{(s+1)}(\mathbb R^L)+\mu_{2k}^{(s+1)}(\mathbb R^L)).
\]
It can thus be checked by direct calculation that $\mathbb E[X_{s+1}\mid X_s=x_k^{(s)}]=x_k^{(s)}$, meaning that $\{X_s\}$ forms a nonnegative martingale, and hence converges a.s. to some $X_\infty$ by the martingale convergence theorem. We call $\{X_s\}$ the SHINE martingale (associated with $\gamma$). Denote by $\mu$ the law of $X_\infty\mathbf1=(X_\infty,\ldots,X_\infty)$.

members.local_label: Theorem 6.7 — Uniform e-power and total-variation separation
members.source_heading: Theorem 6.7 — Uniform e-power and total-variation separation
members.statement_original: There exists an exact bounded e-variable $X$ for $\mathcal P$ against $\mathcal Q$ satisfying $\inf_{Q\in\mathcal Q}\mathbb E^Q[\log X]>0$ if and only if $0\notin\overline{\overline{\operatorname{Span}}\mathcal P+\overline{\operatorname{Conv}}\mathcal Q}$, where the closure is taken with respect to the total variation distance. If $\mathcal Q$ is tight, then we have the further equivalence to $\overline{\operatorname{Span}}\mathcal P\cap\overline{\operatorname{Conv}}\mathcal Q=\varnothing$.
